newsitem.title: UK: Russian military needs urgent rethink - expert.
newsitem.headline: Russian military needs urgent rethink - expert.

text.p: Russia's military, one of the biggest in the world, "is a bit of a mess" because of underfunding and low morale, but could recover with radical reorganisation, a leading expert said on Friday.

Russian Defence Minister Igor Rodionov admitted on Friday that the military was facing "an acute crisis". Chronic underfunding, accommodation problems and lack of up-to-date arms had put it on the edge.
Experts say the Russian armed forces are far too large for the post Cold War world and the military must be cut back and reorganised into more efficient units.
"The whole thing is a bit of a mess," Robert Hall, editor of Jane's Intelligence Review and an expert on Russian military might told Reuters.
"They have not been paid since June. They are in a crisis of reorganisation in the light of their economic problems and they haven't really got a role."
Mark Smith of the Conflicts Studies Research Centre in Sandhurst described Rodionov's comments as dramatic."It is underlining what is becoming an increasing desperate situation for the armed forces."
Russia has about 1,270,000 active members of the armed forces and 20,000,000 in reserve, according to latest figures from the International Institute for Strategic Studies (IISS).
Russia has one of the biggest military forces in the world, with only China and the United States comparable in manpower.

Russia's strategic nuclear forces number 149,000, including 49,000 from the Air Force, Air Defence and the Navy. Although Russia's military spending dropped 15 percent from 1994 to around $82 billion in 1995, it is still a military heavyweight.
"Despite the magnitude of the decline from military superpower status, Russia remains by a clear margin the second largest military spender after the U.S.," IISS said.
The Army, which is divided into eight military districts has 12 tank divisions, 28 motor rifle, five air borne, four machine gun and four artillery divisions.
With 133 submarines, one carrier, 24 cruisers, 21 destroyers, 120 frigates, 80 corvettes, 182 mine warfare vessels and 80 amphibious vessels, Russia's navy is a formidable force.
Rodionov warned that the 1997 military budget covered only a third of necessary expenses and threatened the effectiveness of the armed forces.

"They have got to get a grip," said Hall "and if anybody, Rodionov who is given a very high profile and quality by observers, will get aboard. They have got to cut down their Russian military in a major way if they are going to sustain any professional force at all."
Smith told Reuters Rodionov faced a "gargantuan task".
"That is not to say it can't be done. It's just an enormous task for any leadership."
Hall also cast doubts on the quality of the Russian military and their effectiveness in a major battle, going so far as the predict it would collapse in a major military confrontation.
He said the problem facing the Russians in cutting their forces is what to do with the former soldiers, sailors and pilots because there is no employment and the government cannot pay for them.
"They (the Russians) still have a future in a radically different organisational way. They have got to cut and to reorganise and to do it fairly fast," he added.
